SUMO and the learned model, side by side

The same junction and the same 115 vehicles: same routes, same departure times, same signal plan. In the SUMO panel, SUMO (the teacher the model learned from) drives every car. In the model panel, each car enters under SUMO control for its first few seconds; the Traffic Surrogate Model (seed 2) then drives it in closed loop until the end of its route, and a fixed rule drives it off the map after its exit. Both run on one clock and the same map scale.

Who decides what

Route: every car follows its route from the SUMO scenario in both panels. The model never steers.

Model input: a bird's-eye grid centred on the car (49 × 49 cells of 3 m) holding nearby cars over the last 3 s and the map (lanes, its own route, junction, stop line), plus 64 numbers about the car itself, including the signal state on its route.

Model output: acceleration along the route for the next second (two half-second values). Network: convolutional U-Net, about 2 M parameters, the same for every car.

Entry and exit: each car enters under SUMO control for about 3 s, then the model takes over. At the end of its route, SUMO removes the car; in the model run a fixed rule drives it off the map.

How closely the two runs line up

Same run, same clock, same vehicle IDs, same map coordinates (car body centre). Before take-over, the two positions agree to within 0.00001 m.

After take-over, the runs drift apart. The table shows how far the same car is from its SUMO twin:

after take-overmedian90th pct
0 s0.01 m0.02 m
5 s0.04 m0.13 m
15 s0.44 m3.6 m

This is a closed-loop comparison, not a frame-by-frame prediction test: the other cars are model-driven too, so small differences add up. A car being in a different place is not by itself an error.
